units.translation: Χαλκίδος [of Chalcis], the name of a Scythian city, which Heimsoethius Pr. 420 probably restored in place of Αραβίας [Arabia], about which I have said more in the Preface to the London edition of Prometheus, 1866, p. XIII, and above p. 40.
A clangor at the gates of bronze-bound shields.
And he with bronze-bound sockets makes a din.
and the bronze-thunderbolt lake by Ocean, all-nurturing of the Ethiopians.

It is obscure what χαλκοκέραυνον [bronze-thunderbolt] means, which Wellauer translates as struck by a bronze thunderbolt, endowed with bronze thunderbolts or rich; Todtius p. 17. The conjectures of Both and Hermann, χιλιόκρουνον [with a thousand springs] and χαλκομάραυγον [bronze-gleaming], are hardly probable.
and the bronze-thunderbolt lake by Ocean, all-nurturing of the Ethiopians
Who would say that he discovered bronze, iron, silver, and gold before me?
In the manner of base bronze.
Bronze is a mirror of the form, wine of the mind.
The unharvested bronze of the shield (Blomfield: unharvested of shields) stretched high.
They were struck with bronze-mouthed rams (thus Stanley for ἐμβολαῖς [with rams]).
On the left hand dwell the iron-working Chalybes.

The scholiast says that the Chalybian and Scythian iron does these things. For he has personified the iron, which he says thus moves against the children who wish to divide the property and fight because of it.
A stranger, a settler from Scythia, distributes the lots of steel.
he says that the Chalybian and Scythian iron does these things. For he has personified the iron, which he says thus moves against the children who wish to divide the property and fight because of it
Of the nominative χάλυψ [steel], which Arcadius p. 94, 20 gives, there is one example in Nonnus Dion. 36, 182, few examples of the other cases: see Thes. vol. 8 p. 1285.
For the echo of the clang of steel pierced the recess of the cave.
And all kinds of fruit falling to the ground cause pain.
Do not place your foot on the ground.
A mother's blood on the ground, hard to gather up.
Do not gape at me with a ground-fallen cry like a barbarian man.
Up, house! For too long a time you have lain fallen to the ground.
where it is more probable that it is δροίτης [of a tub] and χαμεύνην [a bed on the ground].
Holding a bed on the ground of a silver-walled tub.
Joy creeps upon me, calling forth a tear.
So as to weep in the eyes from joy.
I raised a cry long ago from joy.
For he led everything from his voice with joy.
Do not be astounded in your mind with joy.
In the first joy of the mouth.
For examples of the word used of the impressed form of a person or thing, see Thes. vol. 8 p. 1311.
